Correlation Measures: a Learning Guide

Nine ways to describe association, with interactive synthetic examples, formulas, worked calculations, and interpretation pitfalls. Each notebook link opens an editable browser version in a new tab. Change code and rerun cells without a local Python installation. Browser preview edits are not saved back to GitHub automatically; save a copy to keep your changes. To explore the collection locally: 
cd marimo-notebooks/correlation_measures
uv run marimo edit
Open summary.py or any of the individual notebooks in the local notebook browser. Public links below open the hosted versions.

Choose a measure

Notebook Data / question Range Main caution
Pearson's r Linear association between numeric variables -1 to +1 Can miss nonlinear dependence; sensitive to outliers
Spearman's rho Monotonic association using ranks -1 to +1 Can miss non-monotonic dependence; use average ranks for ties
Kendall's tau Agreement in pairwise ordering -1 to +1 Tau-b adjusts for ties; its scale differs from Spearman's
Point-biserial correlation One binary variable and one numeric variable -1 to +1 Group coding determines the sign; imbalance affects the value
Phi coefficient Two binary variables -1 to +1 Fixed margins can restrict attainable values
Cramer's V Two categorical variables, without requiring an order 0 to 1 No direction; uncorrected sample V is upward biased
Polychoric correlation Latent normal correlation underlying ordinal categories -1 to +1 Depends on the latent normal and threshold model
Partial correlation Linear association after adjusting both variables for controls -1 to +1 Adjustment is not automatically causal or sufficient
Distance correlation General dependence, including non-monotonic relationships 0 to 1 Sample estimates can be positive under independence
Ranges describe defined coefficients or the model's parameter space; finite samples and fixed margins can limit which values are attainable.

Suggested learning order

Start with Pearson, then compare Spearman and Kendall to see what ranks preserve and discard. Move to point-biserial, phi, and Cramer's V for binary and categorical data. Finally, explore polychoric, partial, and distance correlation for latent variables, adjustment, and more general dependence.

Connections to remember

  • Spearman = Pearson on ranks, with average ranks for tied values.
  • Point-biserial = Pearson with one variable coded 0/1.
  • Phi = Pearson with both variables coded 0/1.
  • Cramer's V = absolute phi for a 2 x 2 table.
  • Partial correlation = Pearson on regression residuals, using the same controls and an intercept in both regressions.
  • Polychoric estimates a latent correlation, not the correlation of arbitrary numeric category codes.

Estimation is not the same as description

Pearson's sample r is the MLE of population correlation under an independent bivariate-normal model with unknown means and variances, for a nondegenerate sample. Sample partial correlation has a related multivariate-normal MLE interpretation under suitable conditions. The polychoric notebook uses two-step estimation, not full joint MLE: it estimates thresholds first, then optimizes the correlation with those thresholds fixed. The other descriptive coefficients should not automatically be called MLEs. Being an MLE does not imply being unbiased.

What no single coefficient tells you

Association is not causation. Inspect plots or contingency tables, consider sample size and uncertainty, and check the assumptions of any inferential procedure. Zero Pearson, Spearman, or Kendall correlation need not mean independence. Population distance correlation is zero exactly under independence for Euclidean random vectors with finite first moments, but a finite-sample estimate alone cannot establish that conclusion. Practice: for each notebook, explain what is measured, calculate the worked example, change the controls, and identify a situation in which the coefficient could mislead. Back to the Notebook Gallery

References and reading guide

Each measure's notebook ends with references and a short explanation of what to read. These links point to original research, books, and author resources rather than unrelated gallery topics.

Research articles by measure

Measure Reading Why it matters
Pearson Pearson (1895), Note on regression and inheritance in the case of two parents Historical regression and correlation foundation
Spearman Spearman (1904), The Proof and Measurement of Association between Two Things Rank correlation foundation
Kendall Kendall (1938), A New Measure of Rank Correlation Pairwise concordance foundation; modern tau-b adjusts for ties
Point-biserial Tate (1954), Correlation Between a Discrete and a Continuous Variable. Point-Biserial Correlation Binary-continuous association
Phi / Cramer's V Bergsma (2013), A bias-correction for Cramer's and Tschuprow's association measures Bias of related unsigned categorical measures, not the historical origin of signed phi
Polychoric Olsson (1979), Maximum Likelihood Estimation of the Polychoric Correlation Coefficient Likelihood-based latent correlation estimation
Partial Baba, Shibata, and Sibuya (2004), Partial Correlation and Conditional Correlation as Measures of Conditional Independence Distinguishing linear adjustment from conditional independence
Distance Szekely, Rizzo, and Bakirov (2007), Measuring and testing dependence by correlation of distances General dependence and independence testing; open-access version

Books

  • Linear and multivariate background: Venables, W. N., and Ripley, B. D. (2002), Modern Applied Statistics with S, 4th edition. Useful alongside Pearson, point-biserial, and partial correlation.
  • Rank-based inference: Hollander, M., Wolfe, D. A., and Chicken, E., Nonparametric Statistical Methods, 3rd edition. Useful alongside Spearman and Kendall.
  • Categorical association: Agresti, A. (2013), Categorical Data Analysis, 3rd edition: author resources. Useful alongside phi and Cramer's V.
  • Ordinal models: Agresti, A. (2010), Analysis of Ordinal Categorical Data, 2nd edition: author resources. Useful alongside polychoric correlation and threshold assumptions.
  • Accessible regression background: James, G., Witten, D., Hastie, T., Tibshirani, R., and Taylor, J. (2023), An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python. The authors provide a free edition; use the regression chapter for background on linear association and adjustment.
DOI links may require a subscription for full text. Author-resource pages provide supporting material, not necessarily the complete book. For distance correlation, start with the open-access research articles rather than expecting a general introductory statistics book to cover it.
